quote: Ueber ein fundamentales Axiom des menschli- chen Verstandes.
english: On a fundamental axiom of human understanding.
topic: Miscellaneous notes: a plan to find a formula for π that might prove its irrationality, questions of reality, a plan to study Schwarz's minimum property of the sphere, a fundamental axiom of human understanding (perhaps that every problem is solvable), and remarks on the concept of integer, continuity and Kant.

triage.modern_statement: This is a programmatic, foundational/philosophical idea rather than one precise theorem. The page summary itself only guesses at the content ('perhaps that every problem is solvable'). If that guess is right, the idea is Hilbert's 'axiom of solvability' (no ignorabimus). It says every definite mathematical problem can be settled by finitely many logical steps: either a solution is found or the problem is proved impossible. Hilbert asks whether this is special to mathematics or a general law of human understanding. In modern terms the closest precise versions are: (a) is every mathematical statement decidable, i.e. provable or refutable, in a suitable formal system? and (b) is there an algorithm that decides first-order validity (the Entscheidungsproblem)?
triage.answered_by: Hilbert published the idea himself in the introduction to his 1900 Paris ICM address 'Mathematical Problems'. He called it the 'axiom of the solvability of every problem' and asked whether it is a general law of the human mind. He restated it in his 1930 Königsberg address ('Wir müssen wissen – wir werden wissen'). The precise formal versions were settled negatively. Gödel's incompleteness theorems were first announced at Königsberg in September 1930 and published in 1931. Church and Turing showed in 1936 that the Entscheidungsproblem is unsolvable. The informal philosophical claim itself is still debated rather than proved or refuted.

evidence.claim: In the 1900 Paris ICM lecture, Hilbert says every definite mathematical problem must be capable of exact settlement, either by an answer or by a proof that it is impossible. He asks whether this 'axiom of the solvability of every problem' belongs only to mathematical thought or is a general law of the nature of the mind. This closely matches the diary wording 'fundamental axiom of human understanding'.

The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy says Hilbert stated in 1900 that there is 'no ignorabimus' in mathematics. He used the phrase repeatedly for his 'conviction of the solvability of every mathematical problem'. The same entry traces this to the Entscheidungsproblem and its negative resolution.
A scholarly article in the Journal of Humanistic Mathematics studies Hilbert's 'axiom of solvability' and how it developed into formal decidability and the decision problem.
Hilbert restated the conviction in his 8 September 1930 Königsberg address with the slogan 'Wir müssen wissen – wir werden wissen'.
Gödel first presented his incompleteness theorems at the Königsberg epistemology conference on 7 September 1930, the day before Hilbert's address.
Hilbert and Ackermann posed the Entscheidungsproblem in 1928. The article says it was shown in 1936 that it cannot be solved (Church and Turing).
Recent logic research still formalizes 'Hilbert's No Ignorabimus Principle' as a decidability principle.

triage.why: The diary note is only a title, and the page summary hedges ('perhaps'), so the identification is not certain. Still, it matches Hilbert's published 1900 wording very closely: he calls solvability an 'axiom' and asks whether it is a general law of the human mind. That makes the axiom of solvability the most likely subject. It is not one of the 23 problems; it is the framing claim of the 1900 address. The precise formal versions were answered negatively by Gödel (1930/31) and by Church and Turing (1936). Whether every mathematical question is solvable in some absolute sense is still a philosophical question, discussed in philosophy of mathematics and in some logic papers. It is not an open mathematical problem in the usual sense, so whether it is 'active today' is unclear.
